cases.title: Rewrite a rough note as a friendly email
cases.task: Turn a blunt note into a warm, clear email under 120 words.
cases.promptWeak: make this an email: budget mtg moved to thu 3pm, need slides from priya before, room changed too
cases.prompt:
Rewrite the following note as a short, friendly email to my team. Keep it under 120 words, keep all facts, and end with one clear request.

Note: budget mtg moved to thu 3pm, need slides from priya before, room changed too (now 4B).
cases.outputWeak:
Subject: Meeting

Hi,

The budget meeting has been moved to Thursday at 3pm. We need slides from Priya before. The room changed too.

Thanks
cases.output:
Subject: Budget meeting — now Thursday 3pm, Room 4B

Hi team,

Quick update: our budget meeting has moved to **Thursday at 3pm**, and we'll now be in **Room 4B**.

Priya — could you share your slides with the group before we meet, so everyone arrives up to speed?

Thanks all — see you Thursday.
notes: The strong prompt names the audience (my team), a length cap, 'keep all facts', and one clear request — four levers from the E3 anatomy.
Notice the weak output silently dropped Room 4B's number and buried the request. Vague prompts don't fail loudly; they fail quietly.
'End with one clear request' is doing heavy lifting: it turns a broadcast into an actionable message.

cases.title: Summarise AND surface what to double-check
cases.task: Get a summary that flags its own weak points instead of hiding them.
cases.prompt:
Summarise the text below in 4 bullet points. Then add a section 'Worth double-checking' listing any specific numbers, names, or claims a careful reader should verify, and why.

Text: The Northfield community solar project, launched in 2023, now supplies power to roughly 1,800 households. Organisers say participation cut average household bills by 18%, and a second phase — adding 2.4 MW of capacity — is planned for late next year pending council approval.
cases.output:
**Summary**
- Northfield's community solar project launched in 2023 and now supplies roughly 1,800 households.
- Organisers report an average household bill reduction of 18%.
- A second phase would add 2.4 MW of capacity.
- Phase two is planned for late next year and still requires council approval.

**Worth double-checking**
- *"roughly 1,800 households"* — a specific figure attributed to no source; confirm with project reports.
- *"cut bills by 18%"* — claimed by organisers, an interested party; look for independent verification.
- *"pending council approval"* — status may have changed since this text was written; check current records.
notes: Asking the model to list what to verify converts E1·L7's three-question habit into part of the output itself.
Note the flag on WHO makes each claim ('organisers say') — attribution-awareness is promptable.
This pattern works on any document: summary + 'worth double-checking' beats summary alone at almost no extra cost.

cases.title: Learn a concept, then get tested on it
cases.task: Turn an assistant into a tutor that checks your understanding.
cases.prompt: Explain what a 'context window' is to a complete beginner, using one everyday analogy, in under 150 words. Then ask me two short questions to check I understood — and wait for my answers before revealing yours.
cases.output:
Imagine talking to someone who can only see the last few pages of your conversation written on a whiteboard. They're brilliant with everything on the board — but anything erased to make room for new writing is simply gone for them.

That whiteboard is a **context window**: the amount of recent text an AI model can consider when it replies. Everything inside it can shape the answer; everything that's slid off it no longer exists for the model. It's why pasting a document into the chat works, and why very long conversations can 'forget' early details — the writing got erased, not the friendship.

**Check your understanding:**
1. Why might an AI 'forget' something from the start of a very long chat?
2. If you want the model to use a document, what's the simplest way to make sure it can?

I'll wait for your answers before sharing mine.
notes: 'Wait for my answers' turns passive reading into active recall — the highest-value study technique there is.
Constraints (one analogy, under 150 words, complete beginner) shape quality more than politeness ever does.
Swap the concept and reuse this prompt for anything you're learning — including the rest of this course.

cases.title: Brainstorm that actually diverges
cases.task: Escape the first-idea rut with structured variety.
cases.promptWeak: give me names for a community tool-lending library
cases.prompt: Suggest 9 names for a community tool-lending library: 3 warm and neighbourly, 3 playful, 3 plain and descriptive. One line each on the feeling it gives. Avoid puns on 'tool time'.
cases.outputWeak:
1. The Tool Shed
2. Tool Time
3. ToolShare
4. The Tool Library
5. Community Tools
6. Tools4All
7. ToolBox
8. Handy Hub
9. The Tool Depot
cases.output:
**Warm & neighbourly**
1. *The Borrowed Barn* — evokes lending between neighbours over a fence.
2. *Many Hands* — cooperative, communal, gently proverbial.
3. *The Share Shed* — friendly alliteration, instantly clear purpose.

**Playful**
4. *Spanner in the Works* — cheeky, memorable, mechanically on-theme.
5. *The Lending Bench* — a pun that works twice (workbench / park bench).
6. *Drill Seekers* — light joke, young energy.

**Plain & descriptive**
7. *Northside Tool Library* — findable, official, grant-application-ready.
8. *Community Tool Share* — says exactly what it is.
9. *The Equipment Commons* — descriptive with a civic, shared-resource note.
notes: Buckets force variety: 3×3 with different tones beats 'give me 9' every time — compare the weak run's near-duplicates.
The exclusion ('avoid puns on tool time') removed the cliché the weak version fell straight into.
'One line on the feeling' makes the list decidable, not just long — you're prompting for your NEXT step, not just output.
